turkey.text: When a female utters a call-note, all the gobblers within hearing return the sound, rolling note after note.

duck.text: Look at that Mallard as he floats on the lake; see his elevated head glittering with emerald-green.

goose.text: Night after night the geese came lumbering in in the dark with a clangor and a whistling of wings.

dove.text: She forces us to forget the chilling blasts of winter, by the soft and melancholy sound of her cooing.

pheasant.text: Stately pheasants, with their glossy feathers shining in the autumn sun.

ruffed-grouse.text: His drum is one of the most welcome and beautiful sounds of spring.

bobwhite.text: Shoot maybe. No shoot, no maybe.

western-quail.text: The grouse and mountain quail, with their broods of precious fluffy chickens.

woodcock.text: He hovers around in a wild, irregular manner, making a sort of murmuring sound; then descends with rapidity as he rose.

snipe.text: They are perhaps the most difficult to shoot of all our birds, as they fly in sudden zigzag lines, and very rapidly.

gray-partridge.text: A partridge will tumble along before a sportsman in order to draw away the dogs from her helpless covey.

ptarmigan.text: Among the barren rocks are Ptarmigan in garments that are painted in the patterns of their rocks.

prairie-chicken.text: Before sunrise, or at the close of day, I heard its curious boomings, witnessed its obstinate battles.

crow.text: The Crow is an extremely shy bird, having found familiarity with man no way to his advantage.

band-tailed-pigeon.text: The air was literally filled with Pigeons; the light of noon-day was obscured as by an eclipse.

tundra-swan.text: Congregating in great flocks, its snowy plumage and musical call notes are pleasing features of this wide water.

sandhill-crane.text: The air was filled with the loud and shrill hooping of the wary sharp-sighted crane.

alligator.text: Clouds of smoke issue from his dilated nostrils. The earth trembles with his thunder.

sage-grouse.text: The guttural booming and clucking of the prairie fowl and the great sage fowl in spring.

sharptail-grouse.text: Prairie fowl swept off, clucking and calling, or strutted about with their sharp tails erect.

spruce-grouse.text: The mountain men call this bird the fool-hen; and most certainly it deserves the name.

deer.text: The white-tail is the most beautiful of all deer when in motion, because of the springy, bounding grace of its trot and canter.

elk.text: The call of the wapiti is one of the grandest and most beautiful sounds in nature.

moose.text: The moose is the giant of all deer; and many hunters esteem it the noblest of American game.

bear.text: Bears are a peaceable people, and mind their own business, instead of going about like the devil seeking whom they may devour.

pronghorn.text: It appeared reather the rappid flight of birds than the motion of quadrupeds.

bighorn-sheep.text: The wild sheep ranks highest among the animal mountaineers of the Sierra.

dall-sheep.text: My success with the white sheep had come only with the hardest kind of work.

mountain-goat.text: Verily the white goat is the fool-hen among beasts of the chase.

mountain-lion.text: The cougar is a very singular beast, shy and elusive to an extraordinary degree.

bison.text: A symbol of the tenacity of wilderness and the destruction of wilderness.

muskox.text: He looked like a South African Buffalo and a Prairie Bison combined, and seemed to get bigger at every moment.

caribou.text: The Caribou is a travelsome beast, always in a hurry, going against the wind.

javelina.text: An enraged Peccary, athirst for blood, is a formidable antagonist.

wild-hog.text: One of the big half-wild boars that ranged free through the woods had no fear of any number of wolves.

wolf.text: Old Lobo was a giant among wolves, and was cunning and strong in proportion to his size.

coyote.text: The cayote is a living, breathing allegory of Want. He is always hungry.

fox.text: The wild, buoyant creature, how beautiful he is!

bobcat.text: Wildlife should be just that, wild.

raccoon.text: In March that brief summary of a bear, the raccoon, comes out of his den in the ledges.

wolverine.text: It is safer to molest a mother Bear than a mother Wolverine when accompanied by the cubs.

marten.text: The Marten is not a poultry-killer, nor a wanton murderer … he lives by honest hunting of wild game.

fisher.text: The fisher, that big sable — almost a wolverine — which preys on everything, from a coon to a fawn.

squirrel.text: He is the mocking-bird of squirrels, pouring forth mixed chatter and song like a perennial fountain.

rabbit.text: The Cottontails had enemies on every side. Their daily life was a series of escapes.

snowshoe-hare.text: Away it scud with an elastic spring over the snow crust, straightening its body and its limbs into graceful length.

ringtail.text: A strange little creature like a small pine marten with a long, bushy tail.
